blocks.text: 6.5.6 Manual Overrides as Fixed Bounds

The optimizer has proposed a plan for GridCap's small portfolio, and the planners have notes on it. Engineering wants the Coast repair P036 in 2028, because the asset failed an inspection. The Valley repair P032 has to wait for a study, so it is out of this plan. No Coast crew is free before 2030, so P021 may not start earlier. And the board wants the Ridge undergrounding P024 in the plan, in whatever year suits. Each note is a **manual override**: a decision a person makes about one project, which the model must respect without being rebuilt. This lesson writes overrides as bounds on the start variables, undoes them, prices them, and checks them against the model's rules, in four rules.
GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio, generated for this course; the overrides are invented for the lesson.
An Override on Start Variables Is a Bound, Not a Row
Every start variable $`x_{i,t}`$ already has bounds: $`0 \le x_{i,t} \le 1`$, with integrality making it 0 or 1. An override that fixes start variables only needs to change those bounds:

items: **Start in year $`y`$**: lower bound of $`x_{i,y}`$ set to 1. The project's once row then forces its other years to 0; setting their upper bounds to 0 as well says so directly.
**Never fund**: upper bound 0 on every $`x_{i,t}`$ of the project.
**Not before year $`y`$**: upper bound 0 on $`x_{i,t}`$ for every $`t < y`$.

blocks.text: None of these adds a row. A bound is part of the variable, so the model's rows stay exactly as the builder wrote them, and an override can never be mistaken for a business rule. The OR-Tools MathOpt sample `time_indexed_scheduling.py` uses the same move for jobs with release times: a start variable for a time before the release gets `upper_bound = 0`.

One kind of override is not about a single variable. **"Fund it, in any year"** is $`\text{started}(i) = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} = 1`$, a rule on a sum, and a sum needs a row. It is the must-do row of lesson 6.5.1, added by a person instead of by the data.
In MathOpt a variable's `lower_bound` and `upper_bound` are properties you can read and set on the model you already built. `overrides.py` applies the planners' four notes to GridCap small:

Three overrides changed only bounds; the fourth, "fund P024", added the one row. The overrides cost $927k of NPV. Two of the results are worth reading closely. P021 was only told "not before 2030", and 2030 is in its window, yet it left the plan: in 2030 it is worth $815k instead of $1,012k in 2029, and the money does more elsewhere. An override says what is allowed; the optimizer still decides. And nine projects the planners never mentioned moved, two of them out of the plan, because the four notes reshaped every year's budget. Show the planner that list, not only the four lines they asked for.
An Override Is Data, and Restoring the Bounds Undoes It
Each call to `apply` returns what it changed: the variable with its old bounds, or the row it added. Undoing an override is putting those back:
The last line of the output above is the model after every override was undone: the same 49 rows and the same $24,260k as before any override. Two things follow, and both matter in a planning tool:

items: **Overrides live outside the model**, as a list of records (who asked, what, when, why), and are applied to a freshly built model or undone from a solved one. Lesson 12.1.2 keeps exactly that list as an audit trail.
**One model serves many what-ifs.** There is no need to rebuild the model to try an override, or to take one back; the next section prices four overrides on one model object.

blocks.text: <!-- practice 1 -->
Price Every Override by Solving With and Without It

An override has a cost, measured the way lesson 6.5.1 measured a mandate's: the best NPV without it, less the best NPV with it. With `apply` and `undo`, every price comes from the same model object, built once:

plan = build(small)                       # built once; every solve below reuses it
free = solve_highs(plan.model).objective_value()
print(f"no override   NPV {money(free)}")
for o in OVERRIDES:
    changes = apply(plan, o)
    value = solve_highs(plan.model).objective_value()
    undo(plan, changes)
    print(f"{o.pid} {o.kind:10} alone  NPV {money(value)}  costs {money(free - value)}")

no override   NPV $24,260k
P036 year       alone  NPV $24,148k  costs $112k
P032 out        alone  NPV $24,148k  costs $112k
P021 not_before alone  NPV $24,139k  costs $121k
P024 in         alone  NPV $23,987k  costs $273k
all four together  NPV $23,333k  costs $927k

One at a time the four cost $112k + $112k + $121k + $273k = $618k; together they cost $927k, half as much again. As with mandates, overrides interact through the budgets they share, so the joint cost has to be measured, never added up. That table is what a planner takes to the meeting: "your four notes cost $927k of value; the board's undergrounding request is the largest single one at $273k".
A Conflicting Override Makes the Model Infeasible, or Quietly Changes It

An override is a person's decision, made without the model's rules in view, and it can contradict them. Some contradictions make the model infeasible; one kind does something worse. Each can be found from the override list and the data alone:

items: **A child forced in while its parent is forced out** breaks the parent rows (lesson 6.5.2).
**Two alternatives forced in** break the alternative row (lesson 6.5.3).
**A must-do forced out** breaks its must row (lesson 6.5.1).

**A start year outside the window** has no variable at all. `apply` sets the upper bound of every year that is not the requested one to 0, and with no variable for the requested year, that forces the project *out*, silently.

blocks.text: `override_conflicts.py` checks four override lists, then applies each and solves:

child in, parent out: ['P023 is forced in, but its parent P022 is forced out']; solve INFEASIBLE
both alternatives in: ["['P030', 'P031'] are forced in, but they are alternatives (G030)"]; solve INFEASIBLE
must-do out: ['P017 is a must-do and cannot be overridden out']; solve INFEASIBLE
outside the window: ['P038 cannot start in 2029: its window is 2027-2027']; solve OPTIMAL with P038 not funded

The first three give the solver's one word, `INFEASIBLE`, where the check gives a sentence a planner can act on. The fourth is the dangerous one: a planner asked for P038 *in*, and the solve is `OPTIMAL` with P038 *out*. Nothing failed, so nothing would be reported. Run the check before every solve with overrides, and refuse an override it flags, rather than letting the model reinterpret it.

As in the earlier lessons of this module, the check is necessary, not sufficient: overrides that pass it can still be infeasible together, for example when the projects forced in cost more than a year's budget. Lesson 9.1.3 finds the rows that conflict when that happens.
<!-- practice 2 -->
The Model
The planning model with the overrides of `overrides.py` marked. Overrides change bounds; only "fund in any year" adds rows.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years of project $`i`$; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$. The overrides: $`O^{\text{yr}}`$ the pairs $`(i, y)`$ "start $`i`$ in year $`y`$", $`O^{\text{out}}`$ the projects never to fund, $`O^{\text{nb}}`$ the pairs $`(i, y)`$ "not before $`y`$", $`O^{\text{in}}`$ the projects to fund in any year.
**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$, with the bounds the overrides set:
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in O^{\text{in}} && \text{(override}_i) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson, a row} \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in g} \text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\textstyle\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \textstyle\sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}

with $`\text{started}(i) = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t}`$. In `overrides.py`, $`O^{\text{yr}} = \{(P036, 2028)\}`$, $`O^{\text{out}} = \{P032\}`$, $`O^{\text{nb}} = \{(P021, 2030)\}`$ and $`O^{\text{in}} = \{P024\}`$; the row is named `override_P024`.
Summary

items: **An override on start variables is a bound, not a row.** Start in a year, never, and not before a year are bounds; "fund in any year" is a sum and needs a row. Here four overrides added one row.
**An override is data, and restoring the bounds undoes it.** Keep overrides as records outside the model; one built model serves every what-if.
**Price every override by solving with and without it.** Four overrides cost $618k one at a time and $927k together.

**A conflicting override makes the model infeasible, or quietly changes it.** Check overrides against windows, must-dos, parents and alternatives before the solve; a year outside the window turned "fund it" into "drop it" with an `OPTIMAL` status.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: a year outside it forces the project out silently
parent not out when the child is in
at most one alternative forced in

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt sample time_indexed_scheduling.py (OR-Tools)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/time_indexed_scheduling.py) (fixes start variables through their bounds for release times, the move overrides make); [MathOpt sample integer_programming.py (OR-Tools)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/integer_programming.py) (checks the termination reason before reading a solution, which an override that makes the model infeasible needs); [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (variable and constraint deletions and incremental solving, the features undoing an override uses).
Challenges

items: Add an override "P036 not after 2028". Which bounds does it change?
In `override_cost.py`, price the overrides in pairs. Which pair interacts the most?
Extend `check` to flag a set of "start in year $`y`$" overrides whose spend in one year is more than that year's budget.

blocks.text: Design Note: Refuse, Don't Reinterpret

A model that quietly turns an impossible override into something possible ("in 2029" into "not at all") hides a disagreement between a person and the data. A planning tool should do the opposite: check every override first, refuse the ones that conflict with a message that names the rule, and apply only the rest. The solver then reports on a model that says what the planners meant, and the audit trail (lesson 12.1.2) records both the overrides that were applied and the ones that were refused, with the reason.
